title: Resolving High-Energy States of Interlayer Excitons in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ Heterostructures
authors: Chirag Chandrakant Palekar, Paulo E. Faria Junior, Tobias Manthei, Maximilian Nagel, Bhabani Sankar Sahoo, Shachi Machchhar, Imad Limame, Martin Podhorský, Jaroslav Fabian, Bárbara Rosa, Stephan Reitzenstein
abstract: High-energy states of interlayer excitons (IXs) in van der Waals heterostructures remain largely unexplored despite their importance for understanding many-body interactions and nonlinear optical phenomena. Here, we use photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy to resolve a Rydberg-like series of excited IX states in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterostructures. We observe multiple PLE resonances below the intralayer exciton energies, which we assign to the 2s-, 3s-, and 4s-like states of the IXs. These resonances are consistently observed across heterostructures with different twist angles, indicating that the high-energy state spectrum is only weakly affected by the twist angle. Wannier-exciton calculations incorporating screened Coulomb interactions reproduce the overall energy scale and qualitative trends of the measured Rydberg-like series, supporting the assignment of the observed resonances. Our findings demonstrate that PLE provides direct experimental access to the previously unexplored high-energy IX states in van der Waals heterostructures.
summary: This work uses PLE spectroscopy to experimentally map the high-energy, Rydberg-like spectrum of interlayer excitons in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterostructures. By comparing these measurements with theoretical calculations, the authors demonstrate that while the excited state energy levels are remarkably stable against changes in twist angle, they are highly sensitive to the surrounding dielectric environment. This confirms PLE as a powerful tool for probing fundamental many-body physics in 2D materials.
main_problem: The high-energy states of interlayer excitons (IXs) in van der Waals heterostructures are largely unexplored, despite their importance for understanding many-body interactions and nonlinear optical phenomena.
main_result: PLE spectroscopy successfully resolves a Rydberg-like series of excited IX states ($2s$-, $3s$-, $4s$-like), demonstrating that the spectrum is robust against twist angle variations but highly sensitive to the dielectric environment.
method: The study combines experimental Photoluminescence Excitation (PLE) spectroscopy with theoretical Wannier-exciton calculations incorporating screened Coulomb interactions.
model_or_system: The physical system is MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ van der Waals heterostructures, which exhibit type-II band alignment leading to interlayer excitons. The analysis models the exciton energy spectrum using effective mass approximations and screened potentials.
key_observables: PLE resonance energies corresponding to $2s$-, $3s$-, and $4s$-like excited IX states; dependence of these energies on twist angle and dielectric screening.
important_parameters: Twist angles (e.g., 1$^\circ$, 14$^\circ$, 56$^\circ$), dielectric environment ($	ext{air/air}$ vs $	ext{hBN/hBN}$), and the principal quantum number ($n$) governing the Rydberg series.
main_assumptions: The observed resonances are assigned to Rydberg-like states based on theoretical models; Wannier-exciton calculations assume parabolic bands and specific screening potentials.
figures_summary: Figures show PLE maps revealing distinct intensity maxima corresponding to $	ext{IX}2$, $	ext{IX}3$, and $	ext{IX}4$. Comparisons illustrate the robustness of these high-energy states across different twist angles versus their sensitivity to dielectric screening in theoretical models.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the experimental feasibility using PLE spectroscopy to map out the previously inaccessible high-energy IX spectrum. It then compares this empirical data against theoretical predictions derived from Wannier-exciton calculations, concluding that environmental screening is the dominant physical factor governing the excited state energy ladder.
why_interesting: The direct spectroscopic access to Rydberg-like excitonic states in solid-state heterostructures bridges concepts from atomic physics (Rydberg atoms) into condensed matter quantum optics. The strong dependence on dielectric environment suggests potential control mechanisms for enhancing nonlinear optical responses.
